studies.title: I Commit My Case To God
studies.meaning: A man inside Pharaoh's own court has been arguing with his people, and this is how he finishes: you will remember what I am telling you, and I hand my affair over to God. The verb means delegating a matter entirely to another's discretion, and the commentators note where it falls. It comes after he has spoken, not instead of speaking. The next line reports the outcome in one clause, and the wording is exact: he was protected from the evils of their scheming, which is narrower than saying no scheme was made.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah gives a long stretch to a believer in Pharaoh's household who had concealed his faith and then spoke openly, and the account is unusual in the Quran for the space it gives to someone who is not a prophet. The Meccan community included people whose safety and livelihood depended on families opposed to the message, so a man arguing inside a hostile house was not a distant figure.

keyTerms.note: To place a matter entirely in someone else's discretion, used of appointing an agent with full authority. It transfers the decision rather than asking for help with it.
Planning carried out out of sight of its target. The word is neutral about the plan's quality and specific about its concealment, which is why what he is protected from is named as its harms.
To encircle and settle upon, used of something coming around on the one who set it going. It describes the scheme completing its circle rather than a punishment arriving from elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: To be an officer or a client in a powerful house meant your income, your safety and your standing all came from the person you might one day have to contradict. In Mecca several early believers were shielded only by a relative who did not share their belief, and others were disowned and lost everything at once. Speaking against your own patron was the most expensive act available to a man in that position.
studies.didYouKnow: This section gives more direct speech to an unnamed believer than the Quran gives to most of the figures it names. He argues across a dozen ayat without ever being identified. The surah is known in the tradition by two names, one taken from a divine attribute in its opening lines and one taken from this man.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The handing over is placed after the speaking, and that order is the whole structure of the passage. Reliance is not offered as an alternative to acting but as what is done with the part that was never yours: he says what has to be said and then delegates the consequences. The protection described afterwards is worded with equal care, covering the harm of the scheme rather than promising that no scheme would be laid.

crossReferences.why: Gives the sentence people said in a comparable position, naming God as the one relied upon.
States the principle plainly: whoever relies on God, He is enough for him, and His command reaches its term.
Records this man's first intervention, made while he was still concealing where he stood.

studies.applyIt: Say the thing you have been not saying, once, to the person who actually needs to hear it. Then stop, and leave what they do with it alone: no follow-up message, no checking how it landed. This passage puts the handing over after the speaking, and most of us reverse the order and then wonder why neither part works.

studies.title: Call On Me And I Answer
studies.meaning: An invitation and a warning share one sentence, and the join between them is where the meaning sits. Call on Me and I will answer you; and those too proud for My worship will enter humbled. The move from calling to worship is doing real work, because it treats asking as itself an act of worship. Refusing to ask is therefore described as arrogance rather than as independence. Commentators note that the answer is promised here without conditions attached, and that other passages supply them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage sits among ayat about people who dispute God's signs with no authority for it, and whose hearts are said to hold only a greatness they will never reach. The surah has been describing Pharaoh's court at length, a place where asking anyone for anything was the shape of weakness. The instruction lands in that setting as the opposite arrangement entirely.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary verb for calling someone by name or inviting them, not a specialised religious term. The Quran uses the same word for summoning a person and for prayer, and the overlap is deliberate.
A form implying a response given to a request that reached the one addressed. It answers the calling directly, which is why the two verbs are set in the same sentence with nothing between them.
From a root meaning to be humbled and shrink. Set against pride in the same ayah, it names the exact reversal of the posture being described, rather than a punishment of another kind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Asking was socially expensive. A man who requested help in public acknowledged a rank beneath the one he asked, and the debt was remembered by everyone present and by their children. Poets were paid to praise patrons partly because praise was the respectable form of asking. In an economy arranged like that, being told that asking is itself the honourable act inverted a scale people lived by daily.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical tradition preserves a report in which supplication is described as being worship itself rather than a part of it, and the commentators cite it precisely when explaining the join in this ayah between calling on God in the first half and worshipping Him in the second. The report and the ayah are read as saying the same thing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Asking is classed as worship, which changes the whole activity. It is not a request submitted to an office and then awaited; the asking is itself the thing that was wanted. That explains why its refusal is named as pride rather than as self-sufficiency, and why the invitation and the warning are put in one sentence instead of two: they describe the same door from either side.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same point from God's side, stating nearness before the response to the caller is described.
Names the specific case, the one driven into a corner, and asks who else answers such a call.
Describes the manner rather than the fact, calling humbly and quietly rather than for an audience.

studies.applyIt: Ask God for one small specific thing today rather than for a general improvement. Name it: the outcome of a particular meeting, patience with one particular person, a sum you actually need. Put it in a sentence short enough to repeat. The ayah promises a response to a call, and a call has to be about something before anything can answer it.
